nameStory: The aromatic aster gets its name from the pleasant fragrance released when you crush or brush against its leaves. This sweet, almost resin-like scent makes it easy to distinguish from other fall-blooming asters that might look similar from a distance.
description: Aromatic aster is a medium-sized wildflower that brightens up late summer and fall with clusters of small purple daisy-like blooms. This herbaceous perennial grows 4-31 inches tall with a somewhat bushy, branching habit. Each flower head has the classic aster look: a yellow center surrounded by narrow purple petals, though the purple can range from light lavender to deep violet.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Crush a leaf between your fingers and smell - you'll detect a sweet, pleasant fragrance that's unmistakable. The leaves are small, narrow, and feel slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple daisy-like flowers with yellow centers bloom in dense clusters from August through November. Each flower head is about half an inch across with 20-30 narrow petals radiating from the center.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, somewhat spreading clump with multiple branching stems that create a rounded overall shape. The plant tends to be wider than it is tall.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small seeds with fluffy white bristles that catch the wind for dispersal, similar to dandelion seeds but much smaller and less noticeable.

habitat: Aromatic aster prefers dry, well-drained soils in open sunny areas like fields, prairies, roadsides, and woodland edges. In New England, you're most likely to spot it in disturbed areas, old fields, and along sunny trail margins where the soil isn't too rich or moist.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of aromatic leaves close to the ground. The distinctive fragrance is already present if you crush the young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Plants develop their full bushy shape and branching structure. Flower buds begin forming in late summer but blooms haven't opened yet.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming season from August through November with masses of purple flowers creating colorful displays. This is the best time to find and identify aromatic aster.
seasonality.winter: Stems turn brown and may persist with fluffy seed heads. The plant dies back to the ground, leaving only dead stems as markers of where it grew.

funFact: Despite being called 'aromatic aster,' this plant is actually more closely related to goldenrods than to the European asters most people think of - scientists recently moved it from the genus Aster to Symphyotrichum based on DNA studies!
confusionNotes: With only 6 recorded observations in New England, aromatic aster is easily confused with the much more common New England aster, which also blooms purple in fall. The key difference is the smell test - crush the leaves and aromatic aster will release its signature sweet fragrance, while New England aster leaves smell more 'green' and unremarkable.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed from Aster oblongifolius to Symphyotrichum oblongifolium, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides. This reflects ongoing research that's reshuffling the aster family based on genetic relationships rather than just appearance.
compareHints: Among its Symphyotrichum relatives in New England, aromatic aster is unique for its distinctive leaf fragrance and relatively uncommon status. While New England aster grows much taller with hairier stems and leaves, and smooth blue aster has broader leaves that clasp the stem, aromatic aster's combination of small rough leaves and sweet scent when crushed makes it unmistakable once you know what to smell for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its many aster relatives, New England aster stands out for its robust size, densely hairy stems, and the distinctive ear-like leaf bases that clasp the stem.
Among its many aster relatives, common blue wood aster stands out with its heart-shaped leaves - most other blue asters like smooth blue aster or New England aster have narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Calico aster stands out from its Symphyotrichum cousins by having much smaller flowers than showy species like New England aster or New York aster.
Among New England's many asters, swamp aster is unique in combining wet habitat preferences with that telltale red-purple stem.
Among New England's many asters, New York aster stands out for its preference for wet habitats and its smooth leaves - many other asters like New England aster have hairy or rough leaves.

Among its many Symphyotrichum relatives, panicled aster stands out for its height and distinctive branching flower arrangement - most other white asters like small white aster have simpler, less elaborate flower clusters.
Among New England's white asters, hairy white oldfield aster stands out for its extremely dense, cloud-like flower clusters and notably fuzzy stems.
Among New England's many asters, perennial saltmarsh aster is unique in its extreme salt tolerance and coastal habitat - no other Symphyotrichum species can survive regular saltwater flooding.
Among its many aster relatives, small white aster stands out for its particularly tiny flowers and smooth stems.
Among New England's many asters, wavy-leaf aster stands out for its distinctive undulating leaf margins - a feature that's much more pronounced than in related species.
Among the white-flowered asters, bushy aster is unique for its extremely compact, mounded growth habit that really does look shrub-like.
Among New England's many asters, white heath aster stands out for its incredibly small, numerous flowers and tiny narrow leaves.
Among its many aster relatives, late purple aster stands out for its extremely open, spreading growth habit - most other Symphyotrichum species grow more upright and dense.
Among New England's many asters, smooth blue aster stands out for its completely hairless, waxy leaves - most other asters have at least some fuzziness.

Among its many aster relatives, annual saltmarsh aster stands out for being truly annual (most others are perennial) and for its extremely small flower heads - much tinier than showy species like New England aster or New York aster.
Eastern silvery aster is easily distinguished from other New England asters by its unique silvery-gray, silky foliage - no other aster in the region has this distinctive texture and color.
Among New England's many Symphyotrichum species, crookedstem aster stands out for its notably thick, often bent stems that turn purple with age.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, Tradescant's aster is distinguished by its coastal preference and salt tolerance, unlike most other Symphyotrichum species that prefer inland habitats.
Among New England's many asters, willowleaf aster stands out for its exceptionally narrow, willow-like leaves - most other Symphyotrichum species have broader, more oval or heart-shaped leaves.
Unlike its robust cousins like New England aster or swamp aster, northern bog aster has a much more delicate, slender build with narrower leaves.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, Ontario aster stands out for its preference for wet bottomlands rather than dry fields or woods.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, shining aster stands out for its exceptionally glossy leaves - most other Symphyotrichum species have fuzzy, rough, or at least matte-finished foliage.
Unlike the robust, hairy New England aster with its deep purple flowers, Anticosti aster is much more delicate with paler blooms.
Unlike its Symphyotrichum relatives such as New England aster or calico aster, rayless annual aster completely lacks ray petals and lives only one year instead of returning each season.

Unlike its common cousin the New England aster with its larger purple flowers and lance-shaped leaves, Lindley's aster has distinctly heart-shaped leaves with fringed edges and smaller, paler blue flowers.
Unlike the heart-shaped leaves of Common Blue Wood Aster or the narrow leaves of panicled aster, arrow-leaved aster's triangular, pointed leaves are unmistakable.
